Solipsism is a philosophical idea — specifically a theory about reality and knowledge — that says: only your own mind can be known to truly exist. Everything outside your mind — other people, the physical world, even your own body — might be nothing more than images, thoughts, or sensations happening inside your consciousness, with no guarantee of any independent reality behind them.

Put even more simply: solipsism is the position that you are the only thing that definitively exists, and the entire universe you seem to experience might just be a vast mental projection — a kind of dream that you are having.

Think about how you experience the world. You see colors, hear sounds, feel textures, taste food, sense pain. But here is the thing: all of these experiences happen inside your mind. Your brain receives signals and constructs the experience of a world for you. You never actually touch "reality" directly — you only ever experience your own perceptions of it.

So how do you know there is a real world out there producing those perceptions? How do you know other people are truly conscious beings who think and feel, rather than just very convincing figures inside your personal mental experience? How do you know the universe existed before you were born, or that it will continue after you are gone?

Solipsism takes these questions seriously and arrives at a startling answer: you don't know, and you can't know. The only thing you can be absolutely certain of is that your own mind exists — because your mind is the one doing all the experiencing, and you cannot step outside it to check what lies beyond.

There are a few ways solipsism can be held as a position, ranging from extreme to moderate.

The strongest and most radical form — often called metaphysical solipsism — says that only you exist, full stop. The external world and other people do not actually exist at all; they are entirely products of your own mind. You are essentially a lone consciousness, generating your entire experienced universe from within yourself.

A somewhat less extreme form — epistemological solipsism — does not necessarily claim that nothing else exists, but insists that you can never know or confirm whether anything outside your mind is real. Perhaps the world is real. Perhaps other people exist. But you have no reliable way of stepping outside your own experience to verify this. Your knowledge is forever trapped inside your own mind, with no exit.

The mildest form — sometimes called methodological solipsism — is less of a sincere belief and more of a technique used by philosophers. It means treating your own subjective experience as the only reliable starting point when examining what we can truly know, without necessarily claiming that nothing else exists. Philosophers sometimes use this as a kind of intellectual reset button — a way of asking, "Okay, stripping everything else away, what can I be truly certain of?"
Why Solipsism Is Almost Impossible to Disprove

This is one of the strangest and most unsettling things about solipsism: nobody has ever produced a completely airtight logical argument against it.

Think about it this way. If you tried to argue against solipsism, any evidence you point to — a book that says solipsism is false, a friend who tells you they are real, a scientific experiment — all of it enters your experience only through your own mind. A committed solipsist can always respond: "Yes, but that book, that friend, that experiment — those are all just part of my mental experience. They don't prove that anything exists outside my mind."

This is why philosophers describe solipsism as "irrefutable" — not because it is correct, but because it is structurally almost impossible to argue against using evidence. Every piece of evidence you produce is filtered through the very mind whose exclusive existence is being debated. You are trying to use the suspected dream to prove there is something outside the dream.

Even René Descartes — the famous philosopher who tried to methodically doubt everything until he reached something absolutely certain — concluded "I think, therefore I am," meaning the only thing he could prove with certainty was that he himself existed, because the very act of doubting proved a doubter was present. But he could not get much further than that without making additional leaps of faith or assumption.
Why Almost No One Actually Believes It

Despite being so difficult to disprove, solipsism is almost universally rejected — including by most philosophers — for a simple practical reason: it is deeply unlivable, and it clashes with everything about how we actually experience the world.

When you stub your toe, the pain is real and immediate. When someone you love dies, the grief is real. When you are hungry, the hunger is real. The world pushes back on us constantly, with a consistency and force that makes it feel overwhelming unlikely to be a projection of our own minds. Other people behave in ways we do not expect, know things we do not know, and surprise us — none of which you would really expect if they were merely creations of your own imagination.

Solipsism also collapses under a strange kind of internal defeat: if only you exist, then the very concept of "other people" becomes meaningless. So does the concept of "truth," since truth would then just be whatever your mind decides. Language itself becomes pointless, because language is built for communication between minds. Most people find these conclusions too absurd to live by, even if they cannot deliver a perfect logical knockout blow against solipsism.

Outside of philosophy, "solipsism" has taken on a looser, more everyday meaning. When someone calls another person "solipsistic," they usually mean that person is profoundly self-absorbed — someone who acts as though only their own experiences, feelings, and opinions are real or matter, and who seems incapable of considering the inner lives of others.

For example: someone who constantly redirects every conversation back to themselves, who seems unable to empathize, who treats the world as a mere backdrop to their own personal story — such a person might be described as solipsistic. It is a stronger and more precise word than "selfish," because it implies the person does not just prioritize themselves, but seems to barely register that other people have their own rich, equally valid inner worlds at all.
How It Relates to Other Ideas

Solipsism sits at the intersection of several major philosophical problems. It is closely tied to skepticism — the broader tradition of questioning what we can truly know about reality. It connects directly to the problem of other minds — the puzzle of how any of us can know that other people are conscious, rather than being very sophisticated biological machines that merely behave as if they are. And it overlaps with idealism — the philosophical view that reality is fundamentally mental in nature rather than physical — though idealism does not necessarily go as far as solipsism does, since many idealists still believe other minds exist.

Solipsism is the claim that your own mind is the only thing whose existence is certain, and that the entire external world — other people, objects, events, the universe itself — may be nothing more than mental experience, with no guaranteed independent reality behind it.

It is more of a philosophical challenge than a seriously held worldview. Its real power lies not in convincing people that they are alone in the universe, but in forcing a genuinely uncomfortable question: what can we actually know for certain, and how do we justify our confidence in an external world and in the reality of other minds? These questions have driven some of the deepest, most rigorous thinking in the entire history of philosophy — and they remain, even today, without a perfectly satisfying answer.

Most people reject solipsism not because they have decisively defeated it with logic, but because they find its conclusion — that you might be the only real thing in existence — too strange, too lonely, and too unworkable to take seriously as a way of living. The questions it raises, however, are ones that anyone thinking carefully about the nature of reality will eventually have to face.
